extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, evolutionary_biologists, and students of natural history
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and lines of evidence for judging whether sexual selection or natural selection (and what form of inheritance) explain sexual differences in colour, ornament, and other structures, chiefly in birds. Focuses on comparative, developmental, behavioral, and domestication evidence used to test hypotheses about sex-limited traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of gradation and known laws of variation as explanatory evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: From the light afforded by the principle of gradation—from what we know of the laws of variation—from the changes which have taken place in many of our domesticated birds—and, lastly, from the character (as we shall hereafter see more clearly) of the immature plumage of young birds—we can sometimes indicate, with a certain amount of confidence, the probable steps by which the males have acquired their brilliant plumage and various ornaments; yet in many cases we are involved in complete darkness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply multiple sources of evidence (gradation, variation laws, domesticated-breed examples, ontogeny/immature plumage) to reconstruct stepwise evolution of ornaments; accept that this approach can sometimes yield probable steps but often leaves uncertainty. Use as corroborative, not definitive, evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexually-limited transmission of successive variations
rubrics_metrics.description: The successive variations have generally been from the first limited in their transmission to the same sex in which they first arose. (Characters which are limited in their development to one sex are always latent in the other.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as a central explanatory criterion: if successive steps are sex-limited from their origin, large male–female differences are readily explained without invoking later natural selection to remove traits in females. Evaluate inheritance patterns and whether traits appear first in one sex and remain confined to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latency of sex-limited characters in the opposite sex
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters which are limited in their development to one sex are always latent in the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for rudimentary or latent expressions of a trait in the opposite sex (e.g., rudiments of spurs in females) as evidence that the trait is sex-limited rather than entirely absent ancestrally; latent expression supports models of sex-limited inheritance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age of appearance of variation predicts transmission pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations which occur late in life are commonly transmitted to the same sex in which they first appear; whilst variations occurring early in life are apt to be transmitted to both sexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ontogenetic timing of trait appearance (juvenile vs adult onset) to predict whether a trait will be sex-limited or shared. For example, ornaments appearing only at sexual maturity in males are more likely to be sex-limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative evidence among related species (inference from variation in allied taxa)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sexes of the several species differ much in length, irrespective of that of the male; and this can be accounted for... by the laws of inheritance—that is by the successive variations having been from the first more or less closely limited in their transmission to the male sex—than by the agency of natural selection, resulting from the length of tail being more or less injurious to the females of these several allied species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare patterns across closely related species (e.g., tail lengths among pheasants) to assess whether differences are better explained by inheritance laws or by direct natural-selection pressures on females. Consistent interspecific patterns favor inheritance explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of domesticated breeds and experimental breeding as tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Our fancier... would have to continue selecting the males during many generations; and each stage of paleness would have to be fixed in the males, and rendered latent in the females... An analogous case has actually occurred, for there are breeds of the pigeon in Belgium... in which the males alone are marked with black striae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine domestic breeding outcomes and artificial-selection experiments for evidence about the ease or difficulty of producing sex-limited traits. Successful or recurrent sex-limited variants in domesticated stocks support the plausibility of similar processes in nature; thought experiments about crossing and reversion are useful to test plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility constraint: difficulty of converting equal transmission into sex-limited transmission by selection
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be an extremely difficult and complex, perhaps an impossible process, to change one form of transmission into the other through selection... without distinct evidence in each case, I am unwilling to admit that this has been effected in natural species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require strong, case-specific evidence before accepting that selection altered the mode of inheritance. Use genetic/ breeding logic: repeated crossing between sexes tending to homogenize traits makes conversion unlikely unless latent tendencies exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether females have been specially modified by natural selection for protection
rubrics_metrics.description: When the sexes of birds differ in colour, it is interesting to determine whether the males alone have been modified by sexual selection... or whether the females have been specially modified through natural selection for the sake of protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish two alternative causal accounts for female dullness: (A) females retained ancestral dullness via natural selection (protective), or (B) males acquired brilliance via sexual selection with inheritance patterns preventing transfer to females. Evaluate nesting ecology, predation risk during incubation, and inheritance evidence to discriminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation between nidification (nest type) and female conspicuousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Wallace: when both sexes are coloured in a very conspicuous manner, the nest is of such a nature as to conceal the sitting bird; but when there is a marked contrast of colour between the sexes, the male being gay and the female dull-coloured, the nest is open and exposes the sitting bird to view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test Wallace's proposed regularity: survey nesting types (open vs concealed/domed/in-holes) across taxa and compare to female conspicuousness. But check for many exceptions; direction of causation may be reversed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for counterexamples and exceptions across taxa
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many exceptions to this view... pigeons... humming-birds... many groups show conspicuous females that build open nests, and inconspicuous females that build concealed nests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single or a few counterexamples can weaken a simple rule; compile broad taxonomic samples and quantify exceptions before accepting or rejecting the proposed generalization. Look for patterns within genera and families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative causality: nesting behavior may follow, not precede, color change
rubrics_metrics.description: It seems to me much more probable that in most cases, as the females were gradually rendered more and more brilliant from partaking of the colours of the male, they were gradually led to change their instincts (supposing that they originally built open nests), and to seek protection by building domed or concealed nests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeing a correlation between female conspicuousness and nest concealment, evaluate whether nesting behavior could have evolved in response to increased conspicuousness (behavioral/instinctual shift) rather than nesting enabling color acquisition. Use historical/phylogenetic and behavioral evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral display and male–male rivalry as indicators of sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: We have... good evidence that humming-birds take especial pains in displaying their tail-feathers;... Two males displaying their charms in front of her... The entertainment would end in a fight between the two performers; but whether the most beautiful or the most pugnacious was the accepted suitor, I know not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct behavioral observations of display, male competition, and female choice (or absence of clear female choice) to infer sexual selection. Note when display leads to fights — sexual selection may act via male rivalry as well as female choice; document which mechanism appears to operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional-cost argument (ecological trade-offs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The long tail of the peacock would be inconvenient and the conspicuous black colour of the male capercailzie dangerous, to the female during the period of incubation: and consequently that the transmission of these characters from the male to the female offspring had been checked through natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ecological/functional costs of a trait for females (e.g., increased predation risk during incubation, cumbersome morphology). If costs are severe, natural selection could oppose trait transmission to females; but evaluate magnitude of cost and inheritance constraints first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudimentary traces as evidence of ancestral presence and transmission patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: When the male is furnished with leg-spurs the female almost always exhibits rudiments of them,—the rudiment sometimes consisting of a mere scale, as in Gallus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for vestigial/rudimentary expressions of male traits in females as evidence of ancestral expression or partial transmission; these traces inform whether loss or sex-limitation better explains current patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ontogenetic and immature-plumage evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: From... the character... of the immature plumage of young birds—we can sometimes indicate... the probable steps by which the males have acquired their brilliant plumage and various ornaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine immature plumage and developmental sequences to infer ancestral states and the timing of trait appearance; ontogenetic stages can reveal latent tendencies and the sequence of trait acquisition.
